name: paste
one_line: merge lines of files side by side
plain: `paste` glues files together line by line, like putting columns next to each other. Line 1 of file A and line 1 of file B become one line separated by a tab.
With -s it does the opposite job: it turns one column into one long row. With -d you choose the separator.
when: Combine a username list and a password list into user:pass pairs.
Turn a column of values into one comma-separated line.
Number lines or pair them up.
Build a CSV from separate lists.

examples.title: Two files side by side
examples.explain: Line 1 of each, joined with a tab, then line 2, and so on.

examples.title: Choose the separator
examples.explain: -d sets the delimiter: here user:password pairs, ready for a credentials list.

examples.title: One column into a row
examples.explain: -s joins all lines of one file into a single line; -d, uses commas. 22, 80, 443 becomes 22,80,443.

examples.title: Pair up lines from one file
examples.explain: Each - reads one line from standard input, so two dashes pair up lines two at a time.

examples.title: Three columns from commands
examples.explain: Process substitution turns commands into files so you can merge their outputs.

examples.title: Several separators in turn
examples.explain: The separator list is used in rotation: first , then ; ...

options.plain: Use these characters instead of a tab, taken in turn.
Paste one file at a time instead of in parallel (join all lines of each file).
Lines end with NUL instead of newline.

mistakes: Files of different length: paste leaves the missing fields empty.
Forgetting that the default separator is a TAB, not a space.
Using -s and expecting columns: it merges lines of each file into one line per file.
Windows line endings (CRLF) inside the files adding stray carriage returns.
try: Combine two small lists with paste -d:.
Pair up lines of a file with paste - -.
